scenes.headline: How a one-prompt deck stages exponential growth
scenes.sub: The Last Boring Slide, by @fluxxrider, and a check of its numbers
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Lectern. This is The Last Boring Slide, a Claude artifact its author says came from one paragraph in about forty minutes.

scenes.quote: I believe you can make it amazing because you have taste and you have the ability. Good luck, Claude.
scenes.say: I believe you can make it amazing because you have taste and you have the ability. Good luck, Claude.

heads: The deck's chart: a linear axis
GPT-6 Astra climbs above the clouds
Astra's interval, and the point beside it
params.floor: everything before 2025 is on the floor

steps.say: The deck draws METR's time horizons on a linear axis. GPT-4 manages four minutes of work. Nearly everything before 2025 lies on the floor.
steps.term: Time horizon: task length finished half the time

steps.say: Then GPT-6 Astra at forty hours, and a dashed line to two hundred hours in July 2027, which is METR's own extrapolation.
Put the same points on a log axis and they sit near a line that steepens only a little. Doubling took about eight months early on, about four and a half lately. The wall is mostly the axis.
METR's appendix gives the forty hours an interval from thirteen to two thousand six hundred and forty-five, and lists Opus five point five next to it at thirty-nine.
Thirty dominoes, each one and a half times the last. Whitehead showed in 1983 a real domino can topple one that big.
steps.caption: height at step n: 1.5 to the power n minus 1, in cm

steps.say: Step thirty is 1.28 kilometres, taller than the Burj Khalifa. Same push, same ratio, thirty times. The arithmetic checks.
Then 2027 on the wall. Every day the same size, until the deck resizes each one by how much progress happens in it.
A label lands on 12 April: AI that beats the best human researchers, from one example run.
steps.caption: one example run, AI Futures Project

left.title: The deck's calendar
items: keeps doubling every 17 days after July
left.say: The calendar's dates are real, from one example run by the AI Futures Project. But its curve keeps doubling every seventeen days after July. Summed, that is about a hundred and fifty thousand years of progress in 2027.

right.title: The forecasters' median
right.say: The same post's median run puts four point two to four point nine years of progress in 2027.

steps.say: The aim slide is plain trigonometry. One degree off is seventeen centimetres at ten metres.
About 6,700 kilometres at the Moon. 4,700 times the Earth to Sun distance at the nearest star. Every number checks.

stations.label: Pre-warm pass
stations.sub: every scene compiled before slide one

stations.label: Render scale
stations.sub: steps down when frames run slow

steps.say: The whole deck is one 5 MB page. Fonts and images ride along as base64.
three.js and the deck's own code are one script.
Every sound, from domino clicks to a choir, is synthesized in code at load.
Before the first slide it compiles every scene behind a loading bar. That is the twenty seconds people saw on phones.
And it drops its resolution when frames run slow, so the talk itself stays smooth.
It ends where it began, on the dull template. A text box types: I have one. Then deletes it.
What do you want? Then the slide tilts by one degree, the aim slide's error applied to the deck itself.

scenes.text: A linear axis turns a gently steepening exponential into a wall. Show this deck with the log axis beside it.
scenes.say: A linear axis turns a gently steepening exponential into a wall. It is a remarkable artifact. Show it with the log axis beside it.

recap: Most numbers check; three need context
scenes.say: One prompt, thirteen scenes. Most of its numbers check. The axis makes the wall.
